---
title: "An Analysis of NYC's Vision Zero Program"
subtitle: "Evaluating the Impact of Traffic Safety Interventions on Pedestrian Casualties (2013-2023)"
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# This chunk loads libraries and prepares all data for the plots and tables.
# It will not be shown on the final webpage.

# 1. LOAD LIBRARIES
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(gt)
library(scales)

# 2. LOAD DATA
vz_data <- read_csv(here::here("data", "input", "intersection_intervention_table_ever_treated_2015-2022.csv"))

# 3. PREPARE DATA FOR PLOT 1: Total Pedestrian Casualties by Year
casualties_by_year <- vz_data %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(total_casualties = sum(pedestrian_death_or_injury, na.rm = TRUE))

# 4. PREPARE DATA FOR THE FACETED CASUALTY TRENDS PLOT
casualties_by_intervention_group <- vz_data %>%
  select(intersection_id, year, pedestrian_death_or_injury, ends_with("_post")) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(ends_with("_post"), -covid_pre_post),
    names_to = "intervention_type",
    values_to = "is_active"
  ) %>%
  group_by(intervention_type, intersection_id) %>%
  mutate(was_ever_treated = max(is_active)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(was_ever_treated == 1) %>%
  group_by(intervention_type, year) %>%
  summarise(total_casualties = sum(pedestrian_death_or_injury, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(
    intervention_type = str_replace_all(intervention_type, "_post", ""),
    intervention_type = str_replace_all(intervention_type, "_", " "),
    intervention_type = str_to_title(intervention_type)
  )

# 5. PREPARE DATA FOR PLOT 2: First-time Interventions (ANY type) by Year
first_treatment_year <- vz_data %>%
  mutate(treatment_count = select(., ends_with("_post")) %>% 
                           select(-speed_limit_post) %>% 
                           rowSums(na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  filter(treatment_count > 0) %>%
  group_by(intersection_id) %>%
  summarise(first_year = min(year, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup()

interventions_by_year <- first_treatment_year %>%
  count(first_year, name = "num_intersections")

# 6. PREPARE DATA FOR THE NINE SMALL PLOTS: First year for EACH intervention type
first_year_by_intervention <- vz_data %>%
  select(intersection_id, year, ends_with("_post")) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(ends_with("_post"), -covid_pre_post),
    names_to = "intervention_type",
    values_to = "is_active"
  ) %>%
  filter(is_active == 1) %>%
  group_by(intersection_id, intervention_type) %>%
  summarise(first_year = min(year), .groups = "drop") %>%
  count(intervention_type, first_year, name = "num_intersections") %>%
  mutate(
    intervention_type = str_replace_all(intervention_type, "_post", ""),
    intervention_type = str_replace_all(intervention_type, "_", " "),
    intervention_type = str_to_title(intervention_type)
  )

# 7. PREPARE DATA FOR THE RESULTS TABLE
regression_results_detailed <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Intervention, ~IRR, ~CI_Lower, ~CI_Upper, ~P_Value,
  "Street Improvement Project Intersection", 1.118, 0.958, 1.305, 0.156,
  "25 MPH Signal Retiming", 1.071, 1.026, 1.118, 0.002,
  "Leading Pedestrian Interval Signal", 1.042, 0.992, 1.095, 0.102,
  "Enhanced Crossing", 1.000, 0.765, 1.308, 0.999,
  "Street Improvement Project Corridor", 0.951, 0.909, 0.995, 0.029,
  "Citywide Speed Limit Reduction", 0.945, 0.900, 0.992, 0.021,
  "Speed Hump", 0.885, 0.815, 0.962, 0.004,
  "Turn Traffic Calming", 0.856, 0.779, 0.941, 0.001,
  "Neighborhood Slow Zone", 0.816, 0.691, 0.964, 0.017
) %>%
  mutate(
    Percent_Change = (IRR - 1),
    CI_Percent_Formatted = paste0(
      "[",
      scales::percent((CI_Lower - 1), accuracy = 0.1),
      ", ",
      scales::percent((CI_Upper - 1), accuracy = 0.1),
      "]"
    )
  )

# 8. PREPARE DATA FOR THE DESCRIPTIVE TABLE
intervention_descriptions <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Intervention, ~Description, ~`Components/ Examples`,
  "Citywide Speed Limit Reduction", "Default speed limit change from 30 MPH to 25 MPH.", "Streets may be signed or unsigned.",
  "Enhanced Crossing", "A marked high-visibility crosswalk on calm streets with low vehicle volumes, high pedestrian traffic, and no traffic signal or stop sign.", "At minimum, include high visibility crosswalk markings, daylighting on all approaches, Americans with Disabilities Act compliant pedestrian ramps, and pedestrian warning signage.",
  "Leading Pedestrian Interval Signal", "Signals that show a pedestrian walk sign before showing a green light to vehicle traffic in the same direction, giving pedestrians a head start to cross the street before car traffic.", NA,
  "Neighborhood Slow Zone", "Neighborhood areas, selected based on crashes, presence of schools, and other factors, in which the speed limit has been reduced to 20 mph.", "Include road markings and signs indicating entrance to a slow zone, along with greater concentration of other interventions.",
  "SIP Corridors", "Safety-oriented engineering improvements that use multiple treatments in a street corridor.", "Examples: large range of subtypes, including markings, vertical elements, signage and regulatory changes, signal changes, concrete, and landscaping.",
  "SIP Intersection", "Safety-oriented engineering improvements that use multiple treatments in a single intersection.", "Same as above, but within intersections rather than along street corridors.",
  "Speed Hump", "A raised area of a roadway designed to reduce vehicle speeds.", NA,
  "Turn Traffic Calming", "A traffic calming measure that guides drivers to turn more safely and increases pedestrian visibility.", "Examples: hardened centerline, slow turn wedge, bike island channelization, median extension.",
  "25 MPH Signal Retiming", "A corridor where the signal progression has been changed to match the 25 MPH speed limit.", NA
)
```

### Vision Zero in New York City

Motor vehicle crashes are a leading cause of death and injury in New York City (NYC). In 2014, the city adopted the **Vision Zero (VZ)** framework, a comprehensive strategy to eliminate all traffic-related fatalities. The program uses a multi-faceted approach, including infrastructure redesign, lower speed limits, and public awareness campaigns. This analysis evaluates the impact of nine distinct street-level interventions on pedestrian casualties. The study examines data from 2013 to 2023, focusing specifically on intersections that received treatments between 2015 and 2021. This approach ensures that every intervention can be evaluated with at least two years of 'before' data and two years of 'after' data, allowing for a robust comparison.

### What Are the Vision Zero Interventions?

The analysis focuses on nine key physical and regulatory changes made to NYC streets. The table below provides a brief description of each intervention.

```{r table-descriptions, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
intervention_descriptions %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_markdown(columns = everything()) %>%
  cols_width(
    Intervention ~ px(180),
    Description ~ px(350),
    everything() ~ px(300)
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    `Components/ Examples` = "Components / Examples"
  ) %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Descriptions of Assessed Vision Zero Interventions"
  ) %>%
  tab_options(
    column_labels.font.weight = "bold"
  )
```

***

### Citywide Pedestrian Casualty Trends

The plot below shows the total annual count of pedestrian casualties (deaths and injuries) across all 9,562 intersections included in our study sample. A notable drop is visible in 2020, likely corresponding to changes in traffic patterns during the COVID-19 pandemic.

```{r plot-casualties, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
ggplot(casualties_by_year, aes(x = year, y = total_casualties)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2013, 2023, by = 2)) +
  labs(
    title = "Annual Pedestrian Casualties in Study Sample (All Intersections)",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Total Pedestrian Casualties"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

The following charts break this down further. Each plot shows the casualty trend for a specific subgroup of intersections: those that **ever** received a particular type of intervention at any point during the study period. This helps to visualize the trends within different intervention cohorts.

```{r plot-casualty-facets, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.height=10, fig.width=9}
ggplot(casualties_by_intervention_group, aes(x = year, y = total_casualties)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ intervention_type, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2013, 2016, 2019, 2022)) +
  labs(
    title = "Annual Pedestrian Casualty Trends by Intervention Group",
    subtitle = "Each plot shows trends for intersections that ever received that treatment",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Total Annual Casualties in Group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

### Vision Zero Implementation Timeline

The Vision Zero program was rolled out in a staggered fashion, with different intersections receiving treatments in different years. The chart below illustrates the number of intersections in our sample that received their first major VZ intervention in each year of the study period (2015-2021). This excludes the citywide speed limit reduction, which was applied to nearly all intersections in 2014.

```{r plot-interventions, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
ggplot(interventions_by_year, aes(x = first_year, y = num_intersections)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkorange", alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_text(aes(label = comma(num_intersections)), vjust = -0.5, size = 3.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2015:2021) +
  labs(
    title = "Number of Intersections Receiving First VZ Treatment",
    subtitle = "Excludes the universal 2014 citywide speed limit reduction",
    x = "Year of First Intervention",
    y = "Number of Unique Intersections"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
```

### Intervention-Specific Rollout

To see how each specific safety measure was rolled out over time, the charts below break down the implementation timeline for each of the nine interventions studied. Each chart shows the number of intersections that received that particular treatment for the first time in a given year. Notice how some interventions, like Signal Retiming, were implemented heavily in certain years, while others, like Enhanced Crossings, were deployed more sparingly.

```{r plot-intervention-facets, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.height=10, fig.width=9}
ggplot(first_year_by_intervention, aes(x = first_year, y = num_intersections)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#008080", alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ intervention_type, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(
    title = "First-Year Implementation for Each Vision Zero Intervention",
    x = "Year of First Implementation",
    y = "Number of Intersections Treated"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()
  )
```

### Impact of VZ Interventions on Pedestrian Safety

We used a negative binomial regression model to estimate the effect of each intervention on the annual count of pedestrian casualties. The table below summarizes these findings. Rows are colored based on the result: **green** for a statistically significant reduction in casualties, **red** for a significant increase, and **grey** for a non-significant result.

```{r table-results, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
regression_results_detailed %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Impact of VZ Interventions on Pedestrian Casualties"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(IRR, P_Value),
    decimals = 3
  ) %>%
  fmt_percent(
    columns = Percent_Change,
    decimals = 2
  ) %>%
  cols_merge_range(
    col_begin = CI_Lower,
    col_end = CI_Upper,
    sep = ", "
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    Intervention = "Intervention",
    IRR = "IRR",
    CI_Lower = "95% CI for IRR",
    Percent_Change = "% Change",
    CI_Percent_Formatted = "95% CI for % Change",
    P_Value = "p-value"
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = list(cell_fill(color = "#e6f5e6"), cell_text(weight = "bold")),
    locations = cells_body(rows = IRR < 1 & P_Value <= 0.05)
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = list(cell_fill(color = "#fee0e2"), cell_text(weight = "bold")),
    locations = cells_body(rows = IRR > 1 & P_Value <= 0.05)
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style = list(cell_fill(color = "#f7f7f7")),
    locations = cells_body(rows = P_Value > 0.05)
  ) %>%
  cols_width(Intervention ~ px(300)) %>%
  tab_options(
    table.border.top.color = "white",
    column_labels.border.bottom.color = "black",
    column_labels.border.bottom.width = px(2)
  )
```

### Ranking Intervention Effectiveness

The bar chart below visualizes the estimated percent change in pedestrian casualties from the table above, ranking the interventions from most protective to most adverse. This provides an at-a-glance summary of which strategies were most effective. The color coding is the same: **green** indicates a significant reduction in casualties, **red** a significant increase, and **grey** no significant effect.

```{r plot-effects, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.height=6, fig.width=9}
results_with_color <- regression_results_detailed %>%
  mutate(
    Significance = case_when(
      P_Value <= 0.05 & Percent_Change < 0 ~ "Significant Reduction",
      P_Value <= 0.05 & Percent_Change > 0 ~ "Significant Increase",
      TRUE ~ "Not Significant"
    )
  )

ggplot(results_with_color, aes(x = Percent_Change, 
                               y = fct_reorder(Intervention, -Percent_Change), 
                               fill = Significance)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent(Percent_Change, accuracy = 0.1)), 
            hjust = ifelse(results_with_color$Percent_Change > 0, -0.1, 1.1),
            size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Significant Reduction" = "#2ca25f", 
                               "Significant Increase" = "#de2d26", 
                               "Not Significant" = "grey80")) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = scales::percent,
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.15, 0.15))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Estimated % Change in Pedestrian Casualties\nby Intervention",
    subtitle = "Interventions are ranked from most effective to least effective",
    x = "% Change in Annual Pedestrian Casualties",
    y = ""
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  )
```

***

### Conclusion

Our analysis indicates that not all Vision Zero interventions are equally effective. The key takeaways are:

*   **Controlling Vehicle Speed is Paramount:** Interventions designed to physically or legally force drivers to slow down are the most successful at reducing pedestrian casualties. **Neighborhood Slow Zones**, **Turn Traffic Calming**, and **Speed Humps** showed the largest protective effects. Effective speed management is the cornerstone of pedestrian safety.

*   **Some Interventions May Have Unintended Consequences:** Retiming traffic signals to create a "green wave" for vehicles traveling 25 MPH was associated with a statistically significant **increase** in pedestrian casualties. This suggests that changes aimed at improving vehicle flow must be carefully evaluated to ensure they do not compromise the safety of other road users.

*   **Systemic Changes Outperform Spot Treatments:** Redesigning an entire street segment (**SIP Corridors**) was found to be effective, while implementing similar projects at a single, isolated **intersection** had no significant impact. This suggests that broader, more comprehensive changes to the streetscape are more impactful.

Ultimately, this research demonstrates that creating a safe transportation system is not at odds with creating an efficient one. Investments that calm traffic are a core component of an efficient network, creating a more predictable and resilient environment for all road users while reducing the profound human and economic costs of traffic collisions.
